facts.statehood_note: Kentucky was carved out of Virginia, which had made it Kentucky County on December 31, 1776. Virginia agreed to statehood on December 18, 1789, and Congress approved it on February 4, 1791. Kentucky entered as a slave state. Its official name is the Commonwealth of Kentucky.
facts.nickname: The Bluegrass State (traditional; never passed into law)
facts.motto: United we stand, divided we fall (adopted 1942); Latin motto Deo gratiam habeamus (2002)
facts.name_origin: Named for the Kentucky River. Where the river's name came from is uncertain; historians have suggested Iroquoian and Algonquian (Shawnee) words.

government.chambers: Kentucky Senate (38 senators, 4-year terms, half elected every two years) and Kentucky House of Representatives (100 representatives, 2-year terms)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; may seek one reelection in a row). The governor leads the executive branch of the Commonwealth.
government.courts: Supreme Court of Kentucky (7 justices), each elected in a nonpartisan election from one of seven Supreme Court districts for an 8-year term. Below it are the Court of Appeals (14 judges, two from each of seven districts), Circuit Courts, and District Courts.
government.local: 120 counties. Pike County is the largest by area and Jefferson County has the most people.
government.constitution: Kentucky's fourth and current constitution was ratified on August 3, 1891 (earlier ones: 1792, 1799, 1850). The earlier constitutions protected slavery; the 1799 constitution took the vote away from free Black men, and the 1850 constitution added even more protections for slavery.
government.kid_line: "All men are, by nature, free and equal" (Section 1)

long_ago.about: Native Americans have lived in Kentucky for more than 14,000 years; Paleoindians arrived around 12,000 BCE. From about 5,000 to 2,000 years ago, Native people explored and mined the upper levels of Mammoth Cave for gypsum and other minerals, using torches.

From about 1000 BCE to 200 CE, Adena people lived as hunter-gatherer-gardeners in extended-family groups of about 15 to 20. They made pottery with Kentucky limestone, built mounds in the Bluegrass, and traded for shells from the Atlantic coast.

From about 900 to 1750 CE, Mississippian farmers grew corn, beans, squash, and gourds and built fortified towns with platform mounds around a plaza, such as Wickliffe (lived in about 1100 to 1350). Fort Ancient peoples in the east lived in permanent villages and used crop rotation and controlled burns.

Shawnee communities farmed corn in summer villages and split into family groups in winter to hunt and make maple sugar; women could serve as chiefs. In the early 1700s, Lower Shawnee Town near present-day South Portsmouth was home to more than 1,200 Shawnee and Six Nations Iroquois people.

The Cherokee hunted in Kentucky and lived in towns of 30 to 60 households, each with a council house and sacred fire. In 1775, in the Treaty of Sycamore Shoals, Cherokee leaders sold land to the Transylvania Land Company.

The Chickasaw held land near where the Ohio and Mississippi Rivers meet. They grew corn and lived in villages with a council house, ball field, and fort, organized into clans traced through the mother's line.

first_peoples.today_note: The federal government does not recognize any tribes in Kentucky, and the state has no process for formal state recognition. Shawnee tribes in Oklahoma, including the Eastern Shawnee, still claim Kentucky as an original homeland. The 2020 Census counted more than 90,000 American Indian and Alaska Native people living in Kentucky. The old idea that Kentucky was only a hunting ground was spread largely by land speculators who wanted it to look empty.
sites: Wickliffe Mounds State Historic Site (Ballard County): a Mississippian village lived in from about 1100 to 1350 CE
Mammoth Cave National Park: Native people mined the cave from about 5,000 to 2,000 years ago; torches and pottery have been found inside

Mantle Rock (Livingston County): on the Trail of Tears in the winter of 1838–39, more than 10,000 Cherokee in 11 groups passed through this area, and some waited here in the cold for the frozen Ohio River to thaw

history.event: Paleoindians, the first people in Kentucky, arrive. Native Americans have lived in Kentucky ever since, for more than 14,000 years.
Adena people make limestone-tempered pottery, build mounds, and trade over long distances.
Mississippian farming towns with platform mounds grow in western and central Kentucky, and Fort Ancient villages grow in the east.
Lower Shawnee Town on the Ohio River is home to more than 1,200 Shawnee and Six Nations Iroquois people.
James Harrod founds Harrod's Town (Harrodsburg). Resettled in March 1775, it becomes the first permanent European settlement in Kentucky.
In the Treaty of Sycamore Shoals, Cherokee leaders sell Kentucky land to the Transylvania Land Company.
Virginia creates Kentucky County. Between 1784 and 1792, ten conventions meet in Danville to plan a separate state.
Kentucky becomes the 15th state, a slave state. Planters in the Bluegrass and the west force enslaved people to grow tobacco and hemp, and Louisville becomes a major slave market.
Abraham Lincoln is born in a one-room log cabin near Hodgenville.

On the Trail of Tears, the U.S. forces more than 10,000 Cherokee west through Kentucky; near Mantle Rock some groups wait in the winter cold for the frozen Ohio River to thaw, and many people die on the journey. In 1838, enslaved guides, including Stephen Bishop, begin leading visitors in Mammoth Cave.

Kentucky declares itself neutral and stays in the Union, though a pro-Confederate convention at Russellville claims secession. The Confederate failure to win the Battle of Perryville on October 8, 1862, Kentucky's largest Civil War battle, keeps Kentucky in the Union.

Black men in Kentucky are allowed to enlist in the Union army, and Camp Nelson becomes a major training site for the U.S. Colored Troops. In November, soldiers force more than 400 of the soldiers' women and children out of camp, and more than 100 die from cold and illness.

On March 3, Congress frees the wives, children, and mothers of U.S. Colored Troops soldiers. By the time the 13th Amendment ends slavery nationwide on December 6, 1865, 23,703 Black men from Kentucky have enlisted.

trailblazers.name: Dragging Canoe
trailblazers.text: The son of the Cherokee leader Attakullakulla (Little Carpenter), he led the opposition to the 1775 Treaty of Sycamore Shoals, which sold central Kentucky lands to Richard Henderson, and warned that the buyers would find a "dark and bloody ground." He then led Cherokee resistance to American settlement until his death in 1792.

trailblazers.name: Stephen Bishop
trailblazers.text: While enslaved, he guided visitors through Mammoth Cave for about 19 years starting in 1838, exploring and naming new passages beyond the Bottomless Pit. In 1842 he drew a map of the cave from memory that was used for more than 40 years. He was freed in 1856.

trailblazers.name: Isaac Murphy
trailblazers.text: Born enslaved in Kentucky in 1861, he became one of the greatest jockeys in history and the first to ride three Kentucky Derby winners (1884, 1890, 1891). In 1955 he was the first jockey voted into the National Museum of Racing and Hall of Fame.

trailblazers.name: Charles Young
trailblazers.text: Born into slavery in Mays Lick, Kentucky, he became the third Black graduate of West Point and the first African American to serve as a national park superintendent. He rose to colonel, the highest-ranking Black officer in the regular army until his death.

trailblazers.name: Carter G. Woodson
trailblazers.text: Called the "Father of African American History," he earned his bachelor's degree from Berea College in Kentucky in 1903 and a doctorate from Harvard in 1912. He founded the Association for the Study of African American Life and History.

trailblazers.name: Alice Dunnigan
trailblazers.text: Born in Russellville, she wrote a newspaper column at age 14 and taught school in Todd County. As a Washington reporter she became the first African American woman to hold a Capitol press pass, and she later wrote The Fascinating Story of Black Kentuckians.

trailblazers.name: Georgia Davis Powers
trailblazers.text: A civil rights organizer who marched for fair laws in Kentucky, she became the first African American to hold a seat in the Kentucky State Senate. Her first bill was a statewide fair housing law, and she served 21 years as a senator.

landforms: Cumberland Plateau and Eastern Coal Field (mountains in the east)
Pottsville Escarpment (sandstone cliffs with rock shelters, waterfalls, and natural bridges)
Black Mountain, the highest point (4,145 feet)
Kentucky Bend, a piece of Kentucky surrounded by Missouri and Tennessee
waters: Cumberland River and Cumberland Falls (67 feet)
geography.regions: Kentucky runs from the Cumberland Plateau mountains and coal fields in the east, through the Knobs and the rolling Bluegrass, to the Pennyroyal Plateau, the Western Coal Field, and the low Jackson Purchase along the Mississippi River.

ecosystems.name: Caves and karst
ecosystems.about: Mammoth Cave has one of the most diverse sets of cave and karst living things in the world, and the park holds more than 1,300 plant species and more than 70 threatened, endangered, or state-listed species.

ecosystems.name: Rivers and freshwater mussels
ecosystems.about: The Green River, which flows through Mammoth Cave National Park, has one of the most diverse populations of freshwater mussels in the eastern United States.

ecosystems.name: Cliffs and forests of the Cumberland Plateau
ecosystems.about: The Pottsville Escarpment is a belt of sandstone cliffs and narrow valleys with rock shelters, waterfalls, and natural bridges, mostly inside Daniel Boone National Forest. Cumberland Falls drops 67 feet into a rocky gorge in a preserve that protects rare plants and animals.

science.weather: Kentucky has a mostly humid subtropical climate with about 46 inches of rain and snow a year. Tornadoes are its deadliest hazard: outbreaks on March 27, 1890, April 3, 1974, and December 10–11, 2021, took many lives. Ice storms also strike, like the January 2009 storm. Temperatures have ranged from 114°F (Greensburg, 1930) to -37°F (Shelbyville, 1994).
science.resources: Kentucky is known for coal (the state mineral), Thoroughbred horses, bourbon, and a history of growing tobacco. Today it ranks fourth in the nation for building cars and trucks and is a leading state for goats and beef cattle.
science.highlight: Mammoth Cave is the world's longest known cave system, mapped and explored at 426 miles, and the exact length is still unknown. It became a World Heritage Site in 1981 and a Biosphere Reserve in 1990.

g3_ss.title: Kentucky's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Frankfort, Louisville, the 120 counties, and the Ohio and Mississippi Rivers, and learn what the General Assembly, governor, and Supreme Court do in the Commonwealth.

g3_ss.title: Kentucky's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Shawnee, Cherokee, and Chickasaw, visit Wickliffe Mounds, and learn why Kentucky was never just a hunting ground.

g3_ss.title: Kentucky Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Meet Dragging Canoe, Stephen Bishop, Isaac Murphy, Charles Young, Alice Dunnigan, and Georgia Davis Powers.

g45_ss.title: Kentucky's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Study Paleoindians, Adena, Mississippian, and Fort Ancient peoples, Lower Shawnee Town, and the Cherokee, Shawnee, and Chickasaw homelands.

g45_ss.title: Settlers, Treaties, and a New State
g45_ss.plan: Trace Harrodsburg, the Treaty of Sycamore Shoals, Kentucky County of Virginia, the Danville conventions, and statehood as a slave state.

g45_ss.title: Kentucky 1792–1877: Slavery, War, and Freedom
g45_ss.plan: Examine slavery on tobacco and hemp farms, the Trail of Tears at Mantle Rock, neutrality and Perryville, Camp Nelson and the U.S. Colored Troops, and the end of slavery in 1865.

g3_sci.title: Inside Mammoth Cave
g3_sci.plan: Explore how caves form in limestone country and which living things make caves their home.

g3_sci.title: Waterfalls and Natural Bridges
g3_sci.plan: Visit Cumberland Falls and the sandstone arches of eastern Kentucky to see how water and weather shape rock.

g3_sci.title: Storm Safety in Kentucky
g3_sci.plan: Learn how tornadoes and ice storms form and how families stay safe.

g45_sci.title: Mapping the Longest Cave
g45_sci.plan: Investigate karst, cave mapping from Stephen Bishop to today, and why the cave keeps getting longer.

g45_sci.title: Mussels of the Green River
g45_sci.plan: Study the Green River's freshwater mussels, how they live, and why protecting rivers matters.

g45_sci.title: Coal and Kentucky's Energy
g45_sci.plan: Learn what coal is, how it is mined, and how mining affects land and water.
